title: Dust and breath (Genesis 2:4–17)
hookLine: God shapes the man from dust and breathes into his nostrils

lines: ASH WEDNESDAY, A LINE OF FOREHEADS.
cards: On Ash Wednesday, a line forms down the middle aisle. One by one, a priest or a minister presses a thumb into a bowl of ashes and draws a cross on each forehead.

One of the phrases said at that moment comes from Genesis: remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return. Hours later, some people are buying coffee with the gray smudge still on. It sounds grim.
But the story it comes from doesn't start with dust and end there. It starts with dust, and then a breath.

teach.b: Genesis now tells creation a second time, up close. Not the wide shot of six days, but a potter at a workbench.

The Douay-Rheims reads: "And the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Slime of the earth is older English for wet clay or soil.
In Hebrew the pun is right on the surface: the man is adam, shaped from the adamah, the ground. An earthling from the earth. Then the breath.
God doesn't speak this one into being.
God leans in close, face to face, and breathes. So the story makes a human out of two things at once: something as ordinary as the dirt under a garden, and something as close as God's own breath.

The Catechism says a human being is one, body and soul together, not a spirit trapped in a shell. The dust matters. Catholics bless bodies, bury them with care, and profess the resurrection of the body.
Last, the garden. God plants a garden in Eden, puts the man there to dress it and keep it, and gives one limit: don't eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

And that ends a week that started on a lookout, opened a library of seventy-three, saw light before the sun, six days and a rest, an image in the square, and now a handful of clay with God's breath in it.

how: On Ash Wednesday Catholics receive ashes on the forehead, sometimes with words drawn from Genesis 3:19, which tells the man he is dust and will return to dust.

the garden God plants in Eden

games.q: what's inside the clay — tap the pairs.

s: the Church teaches the body is just a shell for the soul
the Catechism says a human is one, body and soul together. that's why Catholics believe in the resurrection of the body.
in Hebrew, adam is made from the adamah
the human from the ground: an earthling from the earth.
in Genesis 2, God speaks the first human into being
God forms him from the earth and breathes into his face.

games.q: you're the potter. the clay figure lies finished on the bench, but it doesn't move. what does God do in the story?
o: God commands it to stand up.
God breathes into its face the breath of life.
God leaves it to dry in the sun.
games.why: "and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." not a command this time: a breath, up close.

practice: Take three slow breaths: on the first, notice your body, heavy in the chair, made of the same stuff as the ground; on the second, the air coming in cool and going out warm; on the third, hold both together, dust and breath.
Then keep breathing at your own pace. If you pray, give thanks for the next breath before it comes.

wordCard.voice: Adamah, the ground, in Hebrew: the soil God shapes the first human from, and breathes into, until he becomes a living soul. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the ground, the soil. the first human, adam, is named from it.

carryVoice: Your line: dust that breathes. Both halves, the ground and the breath, held together. That's the week.
